title: Baseboards and Quarter Round: What Happens to Trim During Hardwood Installation?
meta: In a hardwood installation baseboards either stay and get shoe molding or come off and go back over the new floor. Wills Flooring explains Everett options.
keywords: do baseboards need to be removed for hardwood floors, quarter round vs shoe molding hardwood, baseboard removal hardwood installation, hardwood floor expansion gap trim, hardwood floor installation Everett WA
offers: Hardwood floor installation, engineered or solid

blocks.lead: During a hardwood installation the baseboards either stay on the wall and get a new shoe molding or quarter round to cover the expansion gap, or they come off before the floor goes down and go back on top of it for a cleaner, trim-free look.
blocks.detail: Leaving the base on is faster and cheaper. Pulling and resetting costs more labor and some paint touch-up, but it is what most Everett remodels choose because the floor looks built-in rather than added. Either way, door casings are undercut so the boards slide underneath. Wills Flooring installs hardwood at $3.25 per sq ft labor; trim work is quoted with the job at the free estimate.

blocks.html: Trim is the question that comes up at nearly every Everett hardwood estimate, usually as "do you have to take the baseboards off?" The answer depends on the house. A 1990s Silver Lake two-story has thin, painted MDF base that breaks when pried and is cheap to replace. A 1920s Riverside or Bayside bungalow has tall, old-growth fir base with plinth blocks that you would never want to lose. Same job, opposite plan. Here is how we decide, what each option costs you in time and paint, and what to expect on install day.

blocks.text: Why the floor needs a gap at every wall

items.title: Wood moves with the seasons
items.text: Hardwood picks up moisture in an Everett winter and dries in summer. Across a 15 ft room, solid oak can change width by a quarter inch or more. A gap of 1/2 to 3/4 in at every wall gives it somewhere to go instead of buckling.

items.title: Trim hides the gap
items.text: Nobody wants to see a gap, so the base or shoe covers it. The trim is nailed to the wall, never to the floor, so the boards can slide under it freely.

items.title: Nail-down and floating both need it
items.text: Nailed solid floors move less at the edges than floating engineered ones, but both need the gap. Floating floors are the ones that buckle first when someone pins them down with a tight baseboard.

items.title: Door casings get undercut, not trimmed
items.text: Casings are cut with a jamb saw so the flooring slides beneath them. That gives a clean look at every door with no small molding pieces. It happens whether or not the baseboards come off.

blocks.text: What happens on install day if the base comes off

items.text: The paint and caulk line at the top of the base is cut with a knife so the wall paper face does not tear when the base comes away.
Base is pried from the studs with a trim puller, nails pulled through the back, and each piece labeled by wall so it goes back in the same spot.
Boards run to within the expansion gap of the drywall. Casings undercut. Nothing is nailed through the boards at the edges.
Base goes back on the wall, resting on the new floor, nailed to the studs. Old nail holes filled, joints caulked, and the top line re-caulked.
Filled holes and caulk lines need paint. Some homeowners do this themselves; we can include it in the quote.

a.title: Our default when base stays
items: Taller than it is deep, about 3/4 by 1/2 in, so it hugs the base
Looks lighter and more finished than quarter round
Flexes to follow slightly wavy walls and floors
Available in the same species for stain-grade floors
Standard in most Everett homes built after 1980

b.title: Use it when
items: The gap is unusually wide or the old floor was thicker
Matching existing quarter round elsewhere in the house
The base is very short and shoe would look out of scale
Budget rules and it is the cheapest profile
The look is a true 1/4 circle, heavier at the floor line
Pulling MDF base and expecting to reuse it. It snaps at the nail lines and the paper face tears. If the house has MDF, plan on new base or a shoe.
Prying base that has been painted shut without scoring the line. The drywall paper comes with it and now there is a wall repair.
Nailing the shoe into the floor instead of the base. It pins the boards, blocks expansion, and the shoe rides up and down with the floor.
Leaving the old caulk ridge on the wall. Reset base then sits proud at the top and the seam shows.
Forgetting the stair skirt boards and closet interiors, which need the same treatment and are easy to leave off a quote.
Painting the shoe a different white than the base. Ask for the base color name before install day.

blocks.title: Old Everett houses:
blocks.text: Riverside and Bayside homes from the 1900s to 1920s often have 6 to 8 in fir base with plinth blocks at the casings. Do not let anyone replace it. We pull it carefully, reset it over the new floor, and it looks like the floor was always there. The same care applies where new hardwood meets other floors; see our post on transitions and thresholds.

items.html: Check what the base is made of. Press a fingernail into an inconspicuous spot. MDF dents and has no grain; wood does not.
Decide whether you are painting. If the room gets repainted, pulling the base costs you nothing extra in touch-up and is the easy choice.
Measure the old floor thickness. Going from carpet to 3/4 in hardwood changes the height at the base; going from tile can leave a bigger gap that needs shoe even with reset base.
Match species for stain-grade shoe. Natural oak floor, oak shoe. Painted base, primed shoe. Ask which one is on the quote.

Get the trim line in writing. Our quote separates installation labor from removal, reset, new trim and painting so you can choose. The same logic applies to vinyl plank; see baseboards and vinyl plank. Our hardwood installation page covers the rest of the process.

faq.q: Do you have to remove baseboards to install hardwood floors?
faq.a: No. Baseboards can stay on the wall and a shoe molding or quarter round covers the expansion gap. Removing and resetting the base over the new floor gives a cleaner look and is what most Everett remodels choose, but it adds labor and paint touch-up.

faq.q: What is the difference between shoe molding and quarter round?
faq.a: Shoe molding is taller than it is deep, roughly 3/4 by 1/2 in, so it sits close to the base and looks lighter. Quarter round is a true quarter circle, usually 3/4 in each way, and reads heavier. Shoe is our default; quarter round covers wider gaps.

faq.q: Can old baseboards be reused after hardwood installation?
faq.a: Solid wood base almost always can, if it is scored and pried carefully and the nails are pulled through the back. MDF base usually breaks at the nail line and is replaced. We tell you which you have at the estimate.

faq.q: Does removing and reinstalling baseboards cost extra?
faq.a: Yes. The $3.25 per sq ft installation labor covers laying the floor and undercutting door casings. Removal, reset, new trim, shoe molding and painting are separate lines quoted at the free in-home estimate so you can compare the options.

faq.q: Why does new hardwood need a gap at the walls?
faq.a: Wood expands and contracts with humidity. In Everett a solid oak floor can change width noticeably between a wet winter and a dry summer. A 1/2 to 3/4 in gap at every wall lets it move; trim hides the gap and is nailed to the wall, not the floor.

faq.q: Will I need to repaint after the baseboards go back on?
faq.a: Usually some touch-up: filled nail holes and a fresh caulk line at the top of the base. If the base is reset over a thicker floor, a strip of unpainted wall may show and need paint. New base needs full painting.
